sections.title: Mishnah: Kesef, Shtar or Biah; Get or Death; the Yevamah
sections.gist: A woman is acquired through *kesef* (money), *shtar* (a document) or *biah* (intercourse) and acquires herself through a *get* (bill of divorce) or her husband's death; the Mishnah sets the minimum *kesef* and gives the *yevamah* (a brother's childless widow) one way in and two ways out.

bullets.text: *Masechet Kiddushin* has four *perakim* over eighty *dapim*. Its first *perek*, forty *dapim* long, is about *kinyanim* (acquisitions) of every kind: a woman, a *yevamah*, an *eved ivri*, an *eved kena'ani*, real estate and movables.
The later *perakim*: the second opens '*ha'ish mekadesh*' and treats agency at length; the third treats *tena'im* (conditions); the fourth, *asarah yuchasin*, treats lineage.
Every Mishnah in the *masechet* speaks of *kiddushin* (betrothal), *mekadesh* and *mekudeshet*, except this first one. It alone says *niknet*, the language of *kinyan*.

children.title: Kesef, Shtar, Biah: Acts of Kiddushin, Not Nisuin
children.gist: The three ways a woman is acquired, and the shiur's point that each creates *kiddushin*, which forbids her to other men, not *nisuin* (full marriage), the shared life begun at the *chuppah*.

bullets.text: *Ha'ishah niknet bi'shalosh derakhim ve'konah et atzmah bi'shtei derakhim*: a woman is acquired in three ways, through *kesef*, *shtar* and *biah*, and acquires herself in two.

Rashi: '*konah et atzmah*' means *lihyot bi'rshutah*, free *le'hinase le'acher*, to marry another man. He leaves out her vows and her earnings, because those come only with *nisuin*. *Kiddushin* alone only forbids her to other men.
*Kesef*: an object of value given with '*harei at mekudeshet li*' before witnesses. The witnesses make the act binding, not merely provable.
The ring appears nowhere in the Bavli or the Yerushalmi. It is first recorded in *Sefer ha'Chilukim*, which notes that the Jews of Eretz Yisrael used a ring and those of the East did not.
*Shtar*: a document saying '*harei at mekudeshet li*', given before witnesses. It is fully valid, yet there is no evidence it was ever used; the Gemara's stories are all of *kesef*.
*Biah*: a single act done with the intent of creating *kiddushin*, not the ongoing relationship of *nisuin*.

*Kesef*, *shtar* and *biah* are not the ring, the *ketubah* and the *yichud* room: the *ketubah* and *yichud* belong to *nisuin*. Some Genizah *ketubot* (studied by Mordechai Friedman) include '*harei at mekudeshet li*', which suggests some communities blurred the two.

After *kiddushin* she is legally married: another man's *kiddushin* has no effect, relations with another man are adultery, and she needs a *get* to leave. But the couple do not yet live together. That begins with *nisuin* at the *chuppah*, which brings *she'er, kesut ve'onah* and the other mutual obligations treated in *Ketubot*.
The two stages fit a world of early, arranged matches: *kiddushin* bound the parties, and *nisuin* might follow a decade later. Later, *tena'im* with heavy penalties took over that binding role.
*Ketubot* comes before *Kiddushin* only because it is longer; logically *kiddushin* comes first.

children.title: Kesef: A Dinar or a Perutah? Beit Shammai vs. Beit Hillel
children.gist: Beit Shammai require a dinar's worth and Beit Hillel a *perutah*'s worth, one-eighth of an Italian *isar*; the shiur reads the dispute as the moment *kesef* became a symbol.

bullets.text: Beit Shammai: a dinar, or anything worth a dinar. Beit Hillel: a *perutah*, a small copper coin, or anything worth a *perutah*.
How much is a *perutah*? One-eighth of the Italian *isar*.
'Or anything worth it': the *kesef* need not be a coin at all. A copper *perutah* shows that for Beit Hillel *kesef* does not mean silver; it means minimal value.
Naming the Italian *isar* suggests that several kinds of *isar*, of different size and value, were in circulation.
The Mishnah is layered. '*Kesef, shtar u'viah*' is the core statement, the dispute of the schools is a gloss on '*kesef*', and the size of a *perutah* is a gloss on that gloss.

Without the gloss, '*kesef*' would suggest a real price like the Torah's *mohar* (bride-price), fifty *kesef*, which made the act a true *kinyan*. The Sages moved that sum, as two hundred *zuz*, into the *ketubah* (marriage contract), payable at death or divorce.

Once the real payment moved to the *ketubah*, the upfront *kesef* became symbolic, and the schools had to ask how little it could be. Compare real estate, acquired with *kesef* at the market price: no one buys a house with a *perutah*.

children.title: Get or Death; the Yevamah: Biah In, Chalitzah or Death Out
children.gist: A wife goes free by a *get* or her husband's death; a *yevamah* is acquired only by *biah* and goes free by *chalitzah* (the release ceremony) or the *yavam*'s death.

bullets.text: A woman acquires herself through a *get* or through her husband's death.
A *yevamah* is acquired by the *yavam* (her late husband's brother) only through *biah*, and acquires herself through *chalitzah* or the *yavam*'s death.
Already within the first Mishnah the subject moves from the woman to the *yevamah*: the first step in the *perek*'s series of things acquired.

sections.title: Ha'ishah Niknet: Why Kinyan Language, and Why the Woman?
sections.gist: Three questions on the Mishnah's wording: why *kinyan* here but *mekadesh* in the next *perek*, why not *kinyan* there too, and why the woman is the subject; the answers run from Efron's field to *hekdesh* (consecrated property) to her *da'at* (consent).

children.title: Kinyan Because of Kesef: Kichah–Kichah from Efron's Field
children.gist: The Mishnah speaks of *kinyan* because it teaches *kesef*, which a *gezerah shavah* (verbal analogy) on *kichah* (taking) learns from Efron's field, a purchase the Torah calls *kinyan*.

bullets.text: Why does this Mishnah say *ha'ishah niknet*, while the next *perek* (42a) says *ha'ish mekadesh*? Because it wanted to teach *kesef*, the standard means of *kinyan*.

children.title: Ki Yikach and Kach Mimeni: Who Is Taken, and Is Kichah Even Kiddushin?
children.gist: The *gezerah shavah* itself, with the shiur's three difficulties: why it is needed, who 'takes' in each verse, and whether *kichah* in the Torah means *kiddushin* at all.

bullets.text: The source for *kesef*: '*ki yikach ish ishah*' (Devarim 24:1) and '*natati kesef ha'sadeh kach mimeni*' (Bereishit 23:13). Just as Efron's field was acquired with *kesef*, so is a woman.

Tosafot: why is Efron's field needed at all? *Kesef* alone does not prove a *kinyan*, since a payment could work some other way. The *gezerah shavah* makes the *kesef* of *kiddushin* a *kinyan* in the same sense as buying a field.
Tosafot: the match is imperfect. In Bereishit 23:13 what is taken is the silver, which Efron takes; in '*ki yikach ish ishah*' the woman herself is taken.

In the Torah, *kichah* of a woman means *nisuin*, taking her into the household. '*Ve'ish asher yikach et achoto*' speaks of relations, and in '*ki yikach ish ishah u'va eleha*' the coming to her is part of the taking, not a second stage.
The Torah's word for betrothal is *eras*: '*mi ha'ish asher eras ishah ve'lo lekachah*' puts it before *kichah*. So Chazal learn *kiddushin* from verses that, read plainly, speak of *nisuin*.
The Torah's *kinyan* model comes from the *mohar* paid to the father, not from the word *kichah*; the two threads are related but distinct.

children.title: Buying a Field Is Kinyan: Bereishit 25:10 or Yirmeyahu 32:44
children.gist: Two verses show that buying a field with *kesef* is called *kinyan*, so a Mishnah teaching *kesef* says *niknet*.

bullets.text: The Torah calls Efron's field a *kinyan*: '*ha'sadeh asher kanah Avraham*' (Bereishit 25:10).
Alternatively: '*sadot ba'kesef yiknu*' (Yirmeyahu 32:44).
So, since the *tanna* wanted to teach *kesef*, he wrote *ha'ishah niknet*.
Tosafot: one might think Avraham's *kesef* was only the price, and the field passed by *chazakah* (taking possession). '*Sadot ba'kesef yiknu*' shows that the giving of *kesef* itself acquires.

children.title: Lishna de'Oraita or de'Rabbanan: Kiddushin as Hekdesh, and Tosafot's 'Li'
children.gist: The next *perek* switches to the Sages' language, and they call it *kiddushin* because it forbids her to all like *hekdesh*; the shiur adds Tosafot's relational '*li*' and the turn from a *kinyan* model to a *kiddushin* model.

bullets.text: Then let the next *perek* also say *ha'ish koneh*. Answer: the first Mishnah uses *lishna de'Oraita* (the Torah's language), the later one *lishna de'Rabbanan* (the Sages' language).
Why do the Sages call it *kiddushin*? *De'asar lah akulei alma ke'hekdesh*: he makes her forbidden to everyone, like *hekdesh*.
The analogy limps. *Hekdesh* is forbidden even to the one who made it *hekdesh*, and one can make *hekdesh* only of what one owns, while a man does not own the woman before *kiddushin*.
Tosafot on '*li*' in '*harei at mekudeshet li*': she is forbidden to the world because of her bond to me, as things '*mekudashim le'Shamayim*' are forbidden to all because they belong to Heaven.
The shift is from *kinyan*, possession, to *kiddushin*, a status that comes from an exclusive relationship. *Hekdesh* itself can be read as dedication rather than a transfer of ownership.

What would a *kinyan* model give the husband? Not her earnings, which are rabbinic, but perhaps a sexual claim: the Gemara derives his obligation of *onah* from a verse but simply assumes hers. And damages for a miscarriage are paid to the husband.

The early *mishnayot* of the *perek*, each naming an object and its ways of *kinyan*, reflect the *kinyan* model. Moving the real payment into the *ketubah* turned the *kesef* into a symbol, and the institution was renamed *kiddushin*.

children.title: Why the Woman Is the Subject: Her Release or Her Da'at
children.gist: *Ha'ishah niknet* matches '*ve'konah et atzmah*', since '*koneh u'makneh*' fails when the husband dies; or it teaches that *kiddushin* needs her *da'at*.

bullets.text: Then let our Mishnah too say *ha'ish koneh*. Why make the woman the subject?

children.title: Koneh u'Makneh? Not When Heaven Releases Her
children.gist: The woman is the subject because the second clause speaks of her, and the man cannot be named as the one who releases, since death comes from Heaven.

bullets.text: Because the second clause, *ve'konah et atzmah*, speaks of her, the first clause speaks of her too.
Then say *ha'ish koneh u'makneh*: the man acquires and releases, by a *get*. No: when the husband dies it is not he who releases her, but Heaven.
The whole *perek* is built this way: it names the thing acquired (a woman, a *yevamah*, an *eved ivri*, an *eved kena'ani*, real estate) and then lists its ways of *kinyan*.

children.title: Mi'da'atah: Kiddushin Only With Her Da'at, Not Against Her Will
children.gist: '*Ha'ish koneh*' would suggest he could acquire her against her will; '*ha'ishah niknet*' teaches that *kiddushin* takes effect only *mi'da'atah*.

bullets.text: Alternatively: '*ha'ish koneh*' would suggest he can acquire her even against her will. '*Ha'ishah niknet*' teaches: *mi'da'atah*, with her *da'at*, yes; *she'lo mi'da'atah*, no.

In the Torah a father married off his daughter without asking her; only Rivkah's family asks the bride (*nikra la'na'arah ve'nish'alah et pihah*). Chazal limited the father's power to a minor daughter; an adult is married only with her own *da'at*.
So the one Mishnah that speaks the language of *kinyan* is read, at its very first use, as making the woman a subject whose *da'at* is required.

sections.title: Bi'shalosh Derakhim: Why the Feminine 'Three', and Why 'Ways'?
sections.gist: Two questions of wording: whether *derekh* (way) is feminine or masculine, resolved by subject (the Torah and a woman vs. war and a *zav*), and why 'ways' rather than 'matters', which continues past this daf.

children.title: Derekh: Feminine or Masculine? Torah vs. War, a Woman vs. a Zav
children.gist: Verses and *mishnayot* treat *derekh* both ways, and the Gemara reconciles them by subject: the Torah and a woman take the feminine, war and the examination of a *zav* (a man with a genital discharge) the masculine.

children.title: Shalosh vs. Shivah: Verses and Mishnayot in Conflict
children.gist: Shemot 18:20 makes *derekh* feminine, while Devarim 28:7 and the Mishnah on the *zav* make it masculine, so both the verses and the *mishnayot* seem to contradict.

bullets.text: Why *shalosh* and not *sheloshah*? Because the Mishnah says *derekh*, and *derekh* is feminine: '*ve'hodata lahem et ha'derekh yelkhu vah*' (Shemot 18:20), with the feminine *bah*.
Hebrew uses *shalosh* with a feminine noun and *sheloshah* with a masculine one, so the Mishnah's number shows how it treats *derekh*.
Challenge: the Mishnah in Nazir (65b) says *bodkin et ha'zav bi'shivah derakhim*, with the masculine form, not *sheva*.
That Mishnah follows '*be'derekh echad... u've'shivah derakhim yanusu lefanekha*' (Devarim 28:7), where *derekh* is masculine.
Then the verses contradict each other, and so do the two *mishnayot*.

children.title: The Torah and a Woman Feminine, War and the Zav Masculine
children.gist: The gender of *derekh* follows its subject; a *zav* is examined because the cause of a man's discharge matters, while a woman is impure whatever the cause.

bullets.text: The verses: Shemot 18:20 speaks of the way of the Torah, and Torah is feminine ('*Torat Hashem temimah*', Tehillim 19:8). Devarim 28:7 speaks of war, the way of a man and not of a woman, so it is masculine.
The *mishnayot*: ours speaks of a woman, so it is feminine. Examining a *zav* is the way of a man and not of a woman, so it is masculine.
A woman is not examined because she is impure even from causes beyond her control: blood that comes for a reason other than illness still makes her impure.

The examination asks whether a man's discharge was brought on by an outside cause, such as food; if so it is not *zivah* (the discharge of a *zav*) of the Torah. For a woman the cause makes no difference, so there is nothing to examine.

children.title: Derakhim or Devarim? Biah Is Called a Derekh
children.gist: Why not 'three *devarim* (matters)'? Because *biah*, one of the three, is called a *derekh* in Mishlei.

bullets.text: Why say 'ways' at all? Say *devarim*, a masculine noun, with *sheloshah*.
Because the Mishnah wanted to include *biah*, which is called a *derekh*: '*derekh gever be'almah... ken derekh ishah mena'afet*' (Mishlei 30:19–20).

children.continues: Continues in the next lines (2b–3a): why *kesef* and *shtar* are called *derakhim* too, R. Shimon's *baraita* on the *derekh* of a man to pursue a woman, the 'ways' of the *zav* and the *etrog*, and the Gemara's final rule: *derakhim* where there is a distinction, *devarim* where there is none.

key_terms.sense: betrothal, the first stage of marriage
key_terms.definition: The act by which a woman becomes legally married to a man, so that she is forbidden to all other men and needs a get to leave the marriage. It precedes nisuin, when the couple begin living together.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Effected through kesef, shtar or biah; the Gemara explains the Sages' name as making her forbidden to all like hekdesh, and requires her da'at.

key_terms.sense: full marriage, beginning at the chuppah
key_terms.definition: The second stage of marriage, when the bride enters the chuppah and the couple begin a shared household, with the mutual obligations of husband and wife.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The shiur distinguishes it from kiddushin, and notes that the Torah's kichah of a woman refers to nisuin.

key_terms.definition: A formal act that transfers ownership or creates a legal right, such as giving money, writing a document or taking possession.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The opening Mishnah alone uses the language of kinyan for marriage, because it teaches kesef, which is learned from Avraham's purchase of Efron's field.

key_terms.sense: money or an object of value as a mode of acquisition
key_terms.definition: Acquiring by giving money or something of monetary value; one of the standard modes of kinyan, and one of the three ways of effecting kiddushin.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Beit Shammai require a dinar's worth and Beit Hillel a perutah's worth; the Gemara learns kesef for kiddushin from Efron's field.

key_terms.definition: A hermeneutic rule by which a law stated in one passage is applied to another because the same word appears in both.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The shared word kichah links 'ki yikach ish ishah' to Efron's field, teaching that a woman is acquired with kesef.

key_terms.definition: Property dedicated to the Temple or as an offering, which is thereby removed from ordinary use and forbidden for personal benefit.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara explains the name kiddushin: the husband makes her forbidden to everyone like hekdesh.

key_terms.sense: a party's consent to a legal act
key_terms.definition: The knowing will of a party to a transaction, without which the act does not take effect.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Mishnah's 'ha'ishah niknet' teaches that kiddushin takes effect only mi'da'atah, with the woman's consent, and not against her will.

key_terms.sense: a man impure through a genital discharge
key_terms.definition: A man who has an abnormal genital discharge (zivah) and becomes ritually impure; the discharge counts only if it was not brought on by an outside cause.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Mishnah in Nazir about examining a zav in seven ways explains why it says shivah, the masculine form: examination is a man's way.

judgment_calls: The Mishnah is split into three children (the three ways, the kesef dispute, the get and the yevamah). The first two share line 2a.1, but they are distinct topics, and the kesef dispute carries much of the shiur's analysis.
The shiur's long treatment of kiddushin vs. nisuin and of the masechet's structure has no Gemara line of its own. It is folded into the Mishnah sections (s1, s2) rather than made a separate section.

The three wording questions (kinyan here, kiddushin there, the woman as subject) are grouped under one parent (s5), since they all ask why the Mishnah says 'ha'ishah niknet'. They could also stand as three top-level sections.

Tosafot's comments are placed beside the Gemara steps they explain: why the gezerah shavah is needed and who 'takes' in s7, the chazakah point in s8, and 'li' in s9. The essay groups them in a later separate unit.
The shiur's kinyan-model vs. kiddushin-model framing is placed in s9 (the hekdesh explanation) rather than at the Mishnah, because that is where the Gemara itself moves from kinyan to kiddushin.
s17 (derakhim vs. devarim) is placed under the shalosh/derekh parent rather than as its own top-level section, since it continues the same inquiry into the word derekh.
The Gemara's question at 2a.3 is put in the parent s6, with the gezerah shavah (2a.4) and the 'called kinyan' verses (2a.5–2b.1) as its two children.
coverage_notes: The shiur's introduction to the masechet (number of perakim and dapim, the topics of each perek) has no Gemara line; it is included as shiur bullets in s1.

2b.10 (why 'ways' and not 'matters'; biah called a derekh) isn't discussed in the shiur; outlined from the Gemara text only. Since this is the masechet's first daf, there is no previous-daf essay tail to check.

The essay says the Italian isar is a copper coin. The Sefaria translation glosses it as 'a small silver coin', and the Mishnah itself names no metal. The outline gives no metal for the isar; the perutah is called a small copper coin, as in the translation.

The essay describes Tosafot's second question as if Efron says 'take my money'. In Bereishit 23:13 Avraham is speaking and the one who takes the silver is Efron. The outline says 'what is taken is the silver, which Efron takes'.
The essay presents Yirmeyahu 32:44 ('sadot ba'kesef yiknu') as a further confirming verse. The text gives it as an alternative to Bereishit 25:10. Followed the text.

The essay treats the perek's object-by-object structure as the Gemara's 'more substantive' answer to why the woman is the subject. The text's answer is the latter clause ('ve'konah et atzmah'). The structural point is kept as the lecturer's analysis (s11, shiur).
The essay says 'the Gemara is aware' that in the Torah a father married off his daughter without her consent. The text doesn't say this; it is marked as the lecturer's analysis in s12.
The essay discusses the woman's consent (2b.5) before Tosafot's questions on the gezerah shavah (2a.4) and before the kichah discussion. The outline follows the order of the text.

The shiur (and the text through 3a.3) continues past 2b.10: why kesef and shtar are called ways, R. Shimon's baraita, the zav's and etrog's 'ways'. This is outside this daf's scope; noted only in 'continues'.
